hints: Focus on what makes an alcohol primary, secondary or tertiary, it is how many carbons are joined to the carbon bearing the OH group.
Start by listing the four different C5 carbon skeletons and see where you can put an OH to make a $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group for a primary alcohol.
Now place the OH on an internal carbon and check carefully for duplicates by symmetry, then see how many unique secondary positions remain and how many tertiary positions are possible.
walkthrough:
**Recall the classification rule**

Look at the C-OH carbon only. If it is joined to 1 other carbon it is primary, to 2 other carbons it is secondary, to 3 other carbons it is tertiary.

Rule:
$$\text{primary} = \text{RCH}_2\text{OH}, \quad \text{secondary} = \text{R}_2\text{CHOH}, \quad \text{tertiary} = \text{R}_3\text{COH}$$

**Count the primary alcohols**

A primary alcohol needs a $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ end group. There are 4 different ways to have a C5 chain with a $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ end.

They are $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{OH}$. So primary = 4.

**Count the secondary alcohols**

Put OH on a middle carbon joined to two others. This gives pentan-2-ol, pentan-3-ol and 3-methylbutan-2-ol.

Structures:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3, \quad \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3, \quad (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH(OH)CH}_3$$
Note pentan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol are different because the chain is not symmetric when counted from the ends. So secondary = 3.

**Count the tertiary alcohol**

A tertiary alcohol needs a carbon with three alkyl groups plus OH, so $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)-}$. With 5 carbons there is only one way to do this.

It is 2-methylbutan-2-ol:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(OH)(CH}_3)\text{CH}_3$$
So tertiary = 1. That gives 4 primary, 3 secondary, 1 tertiary.

options.A: Incorrect. 3 primary is too few, you have missed one branched $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ isomer, and 2 tertiary is impossible because only 2-methylbutan-2-ol can exist for $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$.
options.B: Incorrect. Primary = 4 is right, but secondary = 2 misses one isomer (pentan-2-ol, pentan-3-ol and 3-methylbutan-2-ol are all distinct) and tertiary = 2 overcounts.
options.C: Correct. Systematic counting gives 4 primary alcohols, 3 secondary alcohols and only 1 tertiary alcohol, 2-methylbutan-2-ol, making 8 structural alcohol isomers in total.
options.D: Incorrect. Primary = 5 overcounts, there are only 4 distinct $\text{RCH}_2\text{OH}$ skeletons, and secondary = 2 undercounts because pentan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol are often mistakenly thought to be the same.
